'''''Juniperus occidentalis''''', known as the '''western juniper''', is a [[shrub]] or tree native to the [[Western United States]], growing in mountains at altitudes of {{convert|800|-|3000|m|sp=us|ft}} and rarely down to {{convert|100|m|ft|abbr=on}}. It is listed as Least Concern on the [[IUCN Red List]] because it is a widespread species with an increasing population.<ref name="iucn status 19 November 2021" />

==Description==
''Juniperus occidentalis'' is a shrub or small tree {{Convert|4–15|m|sp=us}} tall. Exceptionally tall specimens can be found in the [[John Day, Oregon|John Day]] area of Oregon in excess of {{convert|26|–|28|m|ft|abbr=on}} tall.

The shoots are of moderate thickness among [[juniper]]s, at {{Convert|1–1.6|mm|sp=us|frac=32}} diameter. The juvenile [[leaves]] (on young seedlings only) are needle-like and {{Convert|5–10|mm|abbr=on|frac=32}} long. Arranged in [[Phyllotaxis|opposite]] decussate pairs or whorls of three, the adult leaves are scale-like, 1–2 mm long (5 mm on lead shoots) and 1–1.5 mm broad. The [[conifer cone|cones]] are berry-like, 5–10 mm in diameter, blue-brown with a whitish waxy bloom,<ref name=":02">{{Cite book |last1=Arno |first1=Stephen F. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qDD4DwAAQBAJ |title=Northwest Trees: Identifying & Understanding the Region's Native Trees |last2=Hammerly |first2=Ramona P. |publisher=[[Mountaineers Books]] |year=2020 |isbn=978-1-68051-329-5 |edition=field guide |location=Seattle |page=177 |language=en |oclc=1141235469 |orig-date=1977}}</ref> and mature in about 18 months. The male cones are 2–4 mm long and shed their pollen in early spring. The plants are about half [[monoecious]] (with both sexes on the same plant) and half [[dioecious]] (producing cones of only one sex).

The cones contain 1–3 [[seed]]s, the majority of which [[Germination|germinate]] in springtime. In [[Oregon]], where most of the species resides, seeds germinate in April and the foliage emerges in June.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Juniperus occidentalis |url=https://www.fs.fed.us/database/feis/plants/tree/junocc/all.html |access-date=2020-11-24 |website=www.fs.fed.us}}</ref> [[Seed dispersal]] is conducted by water runoff, gravity, and animals.<ref name=":0" />

==Taxonomy==
Further to the south, ''[[Juniperus grandis]]'' (the Sierra juniper) is sometimes treated as a [[Variety (botany)|variety]] of ''J. occidentalis'' (as ''J. occidentalis'' var. ''australis'').<ref name=powo/><ref name=fna/> ''J. grandis'' is {{Convert|12–26|m|abbr=on}} tall with a trunk up to {{Convert|3|m|ft|abbr=on|frac=2}} in diameter. The cones are {{Convert|5–9|mm|abbr=on|frac=32}} wide. Most plants are dioecious, but about 5–10% are monoecious. The two plants are also chemically distinct.<ref>Adams, R. P., S. Nguyen, J. A. Morris and A. E. Schwarzbach. 2006. Re-examination of the taxonomy of the one-seeded, serrate leaf Juniperus of southwestern United States and northern Mexico (Cupressaceae). Phytologia 88(3):299–310.</ref> ''J. grandis'' can be found in California and westernmost Nevada, south of 40° 30' N latitude in the [[Sierra Nevada]] and [[San Bernardino Mountains]]. [[Bennett Juniper|The oldest and largest specimen]] of ''J. grandis'' is {{Convert|26|m|abbr=on}} tall and {{Convert|3.88|m|ftin|abbr=on}} wide, perhaps 3,000 years old, and located in California's [[Stanislaus National Forest]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.conifers.org/cu/ju/australis.htm |title=Conifers.org ''Australis'' |access-date=2006-08-05 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060630173319/http://www.conifers.org/cu/ju/australis.htm |archive-date=2006-06-30 }}</ref>

===Names===
Common names in English for this species include "western juniper", "sierra juniper", "western red cedar", and "yellow cedar". In the United States it is also occasionally called "pencil wood", likely for a common use.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Grandtner |first1=Miroslav M. |title=Elsevier's Dictionary of Trees |date=2005 |publisher=Elsevier |location=Amsterdam, Netherlands |isbn=0-444-51784-7 |page=460 |url=https://archive.org/details/grandtner-m.-elseviers-dictionary-of-trees-1/page/460 |access-date=1 February 2024 |language=English, Latin, French, Spanish |volume=1}}</ref> In the [[Klamath language]] this tree is called ''[[:wikt:q'eeLo|q'eeLo]]''.<ref>{{cite book |publisher=[[Klamath Tribes|The Klamath Tribes]] |date=1989 |title=?ewksiknii?am hemkanks: Klamath Words and Phrases |page=19 |url=https://klamathtribes.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/09/ewksiknii-am-hemkanks-booklet-scan-copy.pdf |access-date=September 16, 2024}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
''J. occidentalis'' can be found in the [[Western United States]]—specifically southeast [[Washington (state)|Washington]], eastern and central Oregon, southwest [[Idaho]], northeastern [[California]] and extreme northwest [[Nevada]], north of 40° 30' N latitude, east of the [[Cascade Range]]. 

It usually occurs on dry, rocky sites where there is less competition from larger species like ponderosa pine and [[coast Douglas-fir]]. Annual precipitation can be as low as {{Convert|20|cm|frac=8}}.<ref name=":02" /> In very exposed positions at high altitude, it can assume a ''[[krummholz]]'' habit, growing low to the ground even when mature with a wide trunk. [[Hybrid (biology)|Hybrids]] with ''[[Juniperus osteosperma|J. osteosperma]]'' are occasionally found.

In the [[John Day, Oregon|John Day]] area of Oregon, it competes for sunlight among [[ponderosa pines]] at the bottom of some deep side canyons. However, it more commonly reaches {{Convert|4–15|m|abbr=on}} with a bushier growth habit on open and barren ground.

==Ecology==
The cones are an important food for several birds, including [[American robin]], [[Clark's nutcracker]], [[phainopepla]] and [[cedar waxwing]]; these digest the fleshy cone scales and disperse the seeds in their droppings.

The plants often bear [[gall]]s caused by the juniper tip midge, ''[[Oligotrophus betheli]]''. These are violet-purple fading to brown, {{Convert|1–2|cm|abbr=on|frac=16}} in diameter, with dense modified spreading scale-leaves {{Convert|6–10|mm|abbr=on|frac=16}} long and 2–3 mm broad at the base.

=== Fire ecology ===
In the past two decades, [[sagebrush steppe]] ecosystems have witnessed an expansion of juniper throughout the western U.S.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last1=Miller|first1=R. F.|last2=Rose|first2=J. A.|date=1999-11-01|title=Fire history and western juniper encroachment in sagebrush steppe.|url=https://journals.uair.arizona.edu/index.php/jrm/article/view/9456|journal=Rangeland Ecology & Management / Journal of Range Management Archives|language=en-US|volume=52|issue=6|pages=550–559|issn=1550-7424}}</ref> This alteration of vegetation change can be associated with the decreased fire frequency, [[overgrazing]] of [[livestock]], and an alteration of climate that transformed into a more wet and mild climate.<ref name=":1" />

Fire scar data was collected and dated to display the expansion of western juniper. It started between 1875 and 1885, with a pinnacle rate of development between approximately 1905 and 1924.<ref name=":1" />

Since the 1990s use of prescribed fires to control expansion of the species has increased. The results of increased prescription fires show a positive effect on plant communities.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Miller|last2=Bates|last3= Svejar|last4=Pierson|first=Richard|first2=Johnathan|first3=Tony|first4=Frederick|date=January 2005|title=Rangeland Ecology and Management of Western Juniper|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/42740730|website=Research Gate}}</ref>

== Uses ==
Like other junipers, ''J. occidentalis'' produces a crop of cones called a [[juniper berry]]. While original European [[gin]]s used berries from ''[[Juniperus communis|J. communis]]'', several distilleries—particularly in [[Bend, Oregon]]—have used local western juniper to flavor their gin.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Stewart |first=Amy |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=SKDzb3BKEWEC |title=The Drunken Botanist |date=2013-03-19 |publisher=Algonquin Books |isbn=978-1-61620-104-3 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Knoll |first=Aaron |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8epqCgAAQBAJ |title=Gin: The Art and Craft of the Artisan Revival |date=2015-09-17 |publisher=Jacqui Small LLP |isbn=978-1-910254-43-1 |language=en}}</ref>

While not common as a [[lumber]] source, [[Oregon State University]] has sponsored research into the use of western juniper for commercial applications such as sign posts and guard rails.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Western Juniper - Lumber Products {{!}} Oregon Wood Innovation Center |url=https://owic.oregonstate.edu/juniper |access-date=2023-02-23 |website=owic.oregonstate.edu}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Homepage {{!}} Western Juniper |url=https://juniper.oregonstate.edu/ |access-date=2023-02-23 |website=juniper.oregonstate.edu}}</ref> Western juniper lumber is noted for its durability and high compression strength.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Burns |first=Jen |date=18 May 2018 |title=The Northwest Juniper Lumber Industry Is Poised For A Healthy Bump |work=Oregon Public Broadcasting |url=https://www.opb.org/news/article/northwest-juniper-lumber-industry/}}</ref>
